card.name: A two‑storey, cream‑brick Dutch‑Colonial home with
card.summary: A two‑storey, cream‑brick Dutch‑Colonial home with a large front porch, three bedrooms, two baths, a garage, and a sleeping porch.
card.description: The residence presents a dignified two‑storey Dutch‑Colonial silhouette, its cream‑colored brick façade rising 488 cm to a gabled roof capped with classic clay tiles. A generous front porch, 300 cm deep and spanning the full 1463 cm width, invites arrival beneath a modest overhang of asphalt shingles, its deck boards of pressure‑treated lumber echoing the sturdy timber of the interior stair. The house offers three well‑proportioned bedrooms, two full baths, a kitchen with maple cabinetry, and a sleeping porch perched above a two‑car garage, all under 2.44 m ceiling heights that preserve the 1920s sense of spaciousness. Double‑hung wood‑frame windows punctuate the brick walls, while a solid wood front door and a steel sectional garage door provide functional contrast. Interior partitions of drywall on timber studs define a living room, dining area with a discreet disappearing bed closet, and a sun‑lit sunroom. The building’s structural system of reinforced‑concrete footings, slab‑on‑grade, and load‑bearing brick walls ensures durability, while modern MEP services are discreetly routed through the walls and roof. The overall composition balances historic charm with contemporary comfort, delivering a home that reads as both a period piece and a livable family dwelling.
plan: Measure the lot dimensions, confirm setbacks, and produce a site‑plan showing the 1463 cm × 1266 cm footprint with a 300 cm deep front porch.
Draft a full‑scale floor plan in CAD, allocating two stories of 244 cm ceiling height, locating three bedrooms, two bathrooms, a kitchen, living room, and a sleeping porch above the garage.
Develop structural drawings for footings, slab‑on‑grade, brick load‑bearing walls, floor joists, and roof trusses, specifying concrete grade and timber sizes.
Coordinate MEP layouts, routing plumbing risers from the kitchen to the bathrooms, installing electrical conduit for lighting and outlets, and sizing HVAC ducts for a two‑story home.
Order all long‑lead items such as windows, doors, garage door, and roof tiles, then schedule trades for foundation, framing, envelope, and interior finishes.
Conduct a final inspection of all systems, verify that the porch roof overhang meets code, and issue a certificate of occupancy.
assumptions: Because the brief did not specify the number of bedrooms, a typical 1920s pattern‑book layout of three bedrooms was chosen.
The wall colour was not given; a traditional cream finish for brick was assumed to match the colonial aesthetic.
A gabled roof with clay tiles was selected as the most common roof type for Dutch‑Colonial homes of the era.
Since no garage size was mentioned, a standard two‑car garage was incorporated, reflecting the Cosgrove reference design.
questions: Do you prefer a specific exterior colour beyond the default cream brick, such as a contrasting trim hue?
Should the porch be fully enclosed with screens or remain an open deck?
Would you like any additional interior features, for example a formal dining room or a dedicated study?

card.name: A one‑storey brick bungalow with a
card.summary: A one‑storey brick bungalow with a large front porch, five rooms, and a kitchen equipped with a full‑size refrigerator.
card.description: The single‑storey, 1,570 cm × 930 cm brick bungalow presents a dignified colonial silhouette with a gable roof clad in dark grey asphalt shingles. Its off‑white brick façade is punctuated by four generous front windows and a solid wooden entry door that swings on a hinge, inviting visitors onto a spacious 300 cm‑deep front porch that stretches the full width of the house. Inside, the layout follows a classic five‑room plan: a bright living room, a well‑appointed kitchen with wood base cabinets and a full‑size 70 cm × 70 cm × 180 cm steel refrigerator, two comfortable bedrooms, and a single bathroom fitted with a ceramic toilet and sink. Interior doors are timber with hinge hardware, and all windows glide on slide tracks for easy ventilation. The hardwood flooring runs continuously from the porch slab through the interior, while the brick exterior walls, 20 cm thick, provide solid thermal mass. Services are discreetly routed: an electrical panel rests on the foundation, and a compact HVAC unit crowns the roof. The overall composition balances historic colonial charm with modern functionality, delivering a welcoming, low‑maintenance home for a small family.
plan: Measure the lot dimensions and confirm the 1570 cm × 930 cm footprint for the house and porch.
Draft a scaled floor plan showing a single‑storey layout with a large front porch, living room, kitchen, two bedrooms, and a bathroom.
Obtain building permits, order structural lumber, brick, roofing, and a standard 70 cm × 70 cm × 180 cm refrigerator.
Excavate, pour a concrete slab foundation, and install floor joists.
Erect brick exterior walls, frame the roof, and attach the gable roof with asphalt shingles.
Finish interior partitions, install doors, windows, kitchen cabinets, the refrigerator, and complete electrical, plumbing, and HVAC.
Perform final inspection and apply exterior paint to the brick.
assumptions: Because the brief did not specify the number of bedrooms, three bedrooms are assumed to provide a typical family layout.
The wall colour is taken as off‑white to complement the brick and match common colonial aesthetics.
A gable roof with asphalt shingles is assumed as the most economical and historically appropriate roofing material.
No garage is included, as the brief made no mention of one, and the chosen reference design (Coloma) does not feature a garage.
questions: What is the orientation of the site and the desired placement of the porch relative to the street?
Do you require any specific utility connections (e.g., gas line for a stove) or energy‑efficiency standards?
Would you like a particular roof pitch or any decorative cornice detail to enhance the colonial character?
